analysis.one_liner: Requires states to provide health insurance to all residents, funded by tobacco, cosmetics, and high-income taxes.
analysis.headline: The universal-coverage bill was referred to two House committees in April 1990 and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before Congress adjourned in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every state to put a health insurance plan in place by 1995 covering all its residents: employers with 25 or more workers would have to enroll employees and their families, states would run subsidized plans with premiums scaled to income for poor and medically uninsurable people, and insurers could not refuse anyone because of a preexisting condition. Medicaid would have had to meet national minimum standards, and states that refused to adopt a plan would risk losing federal Medicaid money. It would have been financed by doubling tobacco excise taxes, adding a 50% tax on cosmetics sales, and raising income taxes at the top.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly tens of millions of Americans who were uninsured or priced out of coverage in 1990 would gain the most: employees of firms with 25 or more workers would get guaranteed coverage, and low-income people, people with preexisting conditions, and the unemployed would get access to plans with premiums proportional to income, caps on deductibles and copays, and no exclusion for preexisting conditions [S2][S3]. Coverage would have included hospital care, doctor visits, screenings, prenatal and well-baby care, mental health care, and long-term care [S3]. State Medicaid programs would have to meet national minimum eligibility and coverage rules, so coverage for the poor would stop varying so much from state to state [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Requires every state to operate a health insurance plan by January 1, 1995 that covers all residents, using an employer mandate for firms with 25 or more employees plus insurance pools for people who work for smaller firms, are self-employed, or are unemployed [S2][S3].

Creates a plan for low-income people, people whom insurers reject because of preexisting conditions, and others who cannot get coverage, with premiums proportional to income and limits on premiums, deductibles, copays, and coinsurance [S3].

Prohibits health plans from excluding or limiting anyone because of any disease, disorder, or condition they have ever had — a protection that did not become federal law until the Affordable Care Act two decades later [S3].

Sets a generous minimum benefit package: inpatient and outpatient hospital and physician care, diagnostic tests, prenatal and well-baby care, at least 45 days of inpatient mental health care and 20 outpatient therapy visits a year, and long-term care including nursing home and home health care [S3].

Requires state Medicaid programs to meet national minimum eligibility and coverage standards set by the Secretary of Health and Human Services, and conditions continued federal Medicaid payments on states adopting a universal plan or one equally effective [S3].

Pays for it with a dedicated Universal Health Coverage Trust Fund funded by doubled tobacco excise taxes, a new 50% cosmetics excise tax, a new 33% income tax bracket, repeal of the phaseout of the 15% rate and personal exemptions (which fell hardest on higher earners), and a change in the maximum capital gains rate [S2][S3].

Authorizes a demonstration program giving extra funds to ten states to reach people with trouble getting affordable care, including rural residents, non-institutionalized elderly and disabled people, and the homeless [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers with 25 or more employees would bear the cost of enrolling workers and their dependents in qualifying health plans [S3]. Tobacco companies and the people who buy their products would pay doubled federal excise taxes — for example, the cigarette tax would double from $8 to $16 per thousand — and cosmetics makers would pay a new 50% excise tax on sales, which would likely be passed on to consumers [S3]. Higher-income households would pay more income tax under the new 33% bracket and the repeal of the phaseout of the 15% rate and personal exemptions [S2][S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Large employers, tobacco users, cosmetics buyers, high earners

drawbacks.text: The employer mandate would impose real costs on firms with 25 or more employees, and the bill allows part-time workers to be charged proportional premiums, which shifts some of the burden onto lower-wage workers [S3].

The 50% excise tax on cosmetics is an unusually steep consumption tax that would likely be passed on to the mostly female consumers who buy these products, and doubled tobacco taxes fall on smokers regardless of income [S3].

The bill requires states to create cost-control 'mechanisms' but specifies none, so it is unclear whether tax revenue would cover the cost of universal coverage, and states that failed could have lost federal Medicaid payments [S3].

The approach is a state-by-state patchwork: quality, premiums, and enforcement could vary widely, and the question of whether coverage should move to federal administration would not be resolved until a 1998 report [S2][S3].
Plans could still use managed care panels and select which providers participate, so some enrollees could face restricted choice of doctors and hospitals [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit was large and concrete: guaranteed coverage for everyone in a state, income-scaled premiums, a ban on preexisting condition exclusions, and a rich minimum benefit package, decades before federal law provided the same protections. The costs were real but conventional for health reform — an employer mandate, higher excise and income taxes — and the weakest parts of the design were the unspecified cost controls and the unfunded risk that states could lose Medicaid money if they could not comply. On the whole it was a straightforward attempt to insure everyone and pay for it visibly, not a badly designed bill, though its state-patchwork structure left real questions about uniformity and financing unanswered.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in two House committees and their health subcommittees from April 1990 until Congress adjourned in January 1991, and no committee or floor vote ever happened.

narrative.text: Rep. David Obey and Rep. Jim McDermott introduced the Universal Health Coverage Act of 1990 in the House on April 18, 1990 [S1][S3].
The same day it was referred jointly to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the House Ways and Means Committee — the two committees that handle health programs and taxes [S5].
Within ten days it was divided among three subcommittees: Health (Ways and Means), and Health and the Environment, and Commerce, Consumer Protection and Competitiveness (Energy and Commerce) [S5].

No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action followed; the last recorded action is the subcommittee referral of April 27, 1990, and the bill died when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The status quo held: insurers kept covering whom they chose with no federal ban on preexisting condition exclusions, employers with 25 or more workers avoided a coverage mandate, high-income households avoided the new 33% bracket and tax changes, and tobacco and cosmetics interests avoided the new excise taxes. The uninsured — roughly 34 million Americans at the time — got nothing.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a House Democrat — one sponsor, one original co-sponsor, and 5 of 257 House Democrats — and no Republican supported it on the record; no vote ever occurred, so a partisan split was never measured.

industries.note: The employer mandate and state insurance pools would have routed millions of new customers into private health plans, locking in private insurance as the permanent channel for universal coverage rather than a public system. In exchange, insurers would have had to accept everyone regardless of preexisting conditions, cover a broad benefit package, and live under premium and cost-sharing caps [S3].

Federal excise taxes would double across the board — cigarettes from $8 to $16 per thousand, cigars, and smokeless tobacco — with a floor-stocks tax on inventory. Much of the burden would fall on smokers, who are disproportionately lower-income, though the revenue would fund coverage for the uninsured [S3].
A new 50% excise tax on the sale price of cosmetics, imposed at the manufacturer level, would likely be passed through to consumers as higher prices, hitting mostly women who buy these products [S3].

Any employer with 25 or more employees, including state and local governments, would have to enroll employees and their families in a qualifying plan and absorb the premium cost. Firms already offering coverage would see little change; firms offering nothing would owe new spending [S3].

The bill creates a 33% tax bracket for top incomes, repeals the phaseout of the 15% rate and personal exemptions (a tax increase on upper earners), and changes the maximum capital gains rate — the first substantial top-rate increases after the 1986 tax act [S2][S3].
